docs.title: Crosswork CNC Hands-on
docs.text:
This is the operator lab for Cisco Crosswork Network Controller (CNC) 7.2.1-SP. You will use the dCloud session from chapter 1: one CNC, a five-node IOS-XR lab, and a dedicated SR-PCE lab.

Each chapter has an objective, the clicks or CLI, the result you should see, and a short Done when list. Router work in this lab is show output unless a chapter says otherwise. Configuration changes go through CNC.

docs.title: Lab story
docs.text:
1. Bring CNC out of maintenance and start both CML labs.
  2. Confirm CNC, the providers, and collection are healthy.
  3. Read the topology in the UI and confirm it from XR CLI.
  4. Walk inventory, faults, configuration, and performance, mapped to the SolarWinds views operations already uses.
  5. Observe a PCC-initiated SR policy, then create a PCE-initiated SRv6 policy.
  6. Provision an L3VPN and steer it onto that policy.
  7. Provision a VPWS L2VPN. VPLS, an NSO custom template, and sync-from are optional.
  8. Enable Service Health on the VPWS you created.
  9. Collect showtech, read collection jobs and alarms, and walk the patch screen.
  10. Optional: ask the CNC MCP assistant one inventory question.

docs.title: Lab values
docs.text:
Copy this table into your notes. Fill hostnames and interfaces from the CML labs and from the instructor. Keep passwords out of the guide, out of chat, and out of screenshots you share.

Item Your value CNC UI https://[2001:db8:134::200]:30603 (from chapter 1) XR CML lab 5-nodes_L3VPN 8201-32FH 25.3.1-ipv6 PCE CML lab xrv9k-25.4.1-pce-for-CNC7.2-ipv6 Headend PE Endpoint PE Attachment interfaces PCE-initiated policy name pta-pce-01 Policy color assigned by the instructor L3VPN name pta-l3vpn-01 VPWS name pta-vpws-01

docs.title: How to read this guide
docs.text:
From this folder, with the existing virtual environment:

source venv/bin/activate
mkdocs serve

Open the local URL MkDocs prints. mkdocs build writes the static site under site/.

docs.title: 1. Preparation
docs.text:
Time: 20 minutes, most of it waiting.

Objective: Leave maintenance mode, start the CML lab, and log in to a controller that is ready for work.

Instructor

Maintenance mode shuts the applications down gracefully, and bringing them back takes several minutes.

docs.title: 1.1 Disable maintenance mode
docs.text:
Maintenance mode is how CNC stops itself cleanly for a reboot, a backup, or a restore. After a reboot that began in maintenance mode, the cluster comes back in maintenance mode and waits for the slider to be turned off.

  1. Sign in to the dCloud.

  2. Access Ubuntu2204-1T-Desktop, run Firefox on the Desktop and open CNC UI (username and password are shared in the session)

    https://[2001:db8:134::200]:30603

  3. Go to Administration > Settings > System Settings > Maintenance Mode.

  4. If a popup already offers to turn maintenance mode off, accept it.

  5. If the Maintenance slider is On, drag it to Off and confirm.

  6. Wait. The applications need several minutes.

Result: The maintenance slider stays Off, the UI loads the normal home page.

docs.title: 1.2 Start the CML lab
docs.text:
1. Open another tab on Firefox and click "CML2 for XR" in the bookmark.
  2. Start "5-nodes_L3VPN 8201-32FH 25.3.1-ipv6" scenario
  3. Open another tab on Firefox and click "CML2 for PCE" in the bookmark.
  4. Start "xrv9k-25.4.1-pce-for-CNC7.2-ipv6" scenario

Result: The lab is booted. CNC can reach the devices after the providers and the Data Gateway are healthy. You confirm that reachability in the next chapter.

Result: You are in the UI as yourself, and the controller is in normal operating mode.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Maintenance mode is Off.
  • Log in to CNC
  • The CML labs are booted.

docs.title: 2. CNC management
docs.text:
Time: 30 minutes.

Objective: Confirm that CNC 7.2 is healthy enough for topology, inventory, traffic engineering, and service provisioning. You are reading the system, not rebuilding it.

The rest of the lab depends on three things:

Later work Depends on Topology and SR policies SR-PCE provider, BGP-LS and PCEP from the routers Inventory, alarms, interface counters Data Gateway collection jobs L3VPN and L2VPN provisioning NSO provider, devices in sync

docs.title: 2.1 Crosswork Summary and Crosswork Health
docs.text:
1. From the main menu, go to Administration > Crosswork Manager.
  2. Stay on the Crosswork Summary tab. Read the tiles for the cluster (or single VM), Platform Infrastructure, and the installed applications.
  3. Open System summary. Confirm the VM is up and that CPU, memory, and disk are not in a warning state.
  4. Open the Crosswork Health tab.
  5. For each of the following applications, open the tile and confirm the application (and its microservices) are Healthy or Running:
    • Platform Infrastructure
    • Optimization Engine
    • Active Topology
    • Element Management Functions / Device Lifecycle Management
    • Service Health, if it is installed (chapter 8 uses it)
  6. Open Alarms or Events on an application tile only far enough to see whether anything is raised against the platform itself. Device alarms belong in chapter 4 and chapter 9.

Result: You can name the applications this lab uses and their health state.

Leave restart, drain, and maintenance controls untouched. You already left maintenance mode in chapter 1.

docs.title: 2.2 Providers
docs.text:
CNC learns the routed topology from SR-PCE. CNC provisions services through NSO. Both are providers.

  1. Go to Administration > Manage Provider Access.
  2. Find the SR-PCE provider that points at the PCE CML lab (xrv9k-25.4.1-pce-for-CNC7.2-ipv6). Read reachability and the protocol state. You want the provider reachable, with the topology feed up.
  3. Find the NSO provider. Read reachability. You want NSO reachable.
  4. Open a provider only far enough to see the credential profile name. The profile is a pointer. The password stays in the profile store.

Result: SR-PCE and NSO are both reachable.

If SR-PCE is down, stop before chapter 3. If NSO is down, you can still walk topology and element management; wait until NSO is reachable before chapters 6 and 7.

docs.title: 2.3 Data Gateway and collection at a glance
docs.text:
Interface counters, inventory detail, syslog, and SNMP traps arrive through a Crosswork Data Gateway (CDG). This dCloud session may use a dedicated Data Gateway VM or the embedded collector on a single VM. Either way, devices must be attached and collection must be running.

  1. Go to Administration > Data Gateway Management.
  2. Confirm the gateway (or pool) is enrolled and administratively Up.
  3. Open the gateway and confirm the XR lab devices are attached to it.
  4. Open Administration > Collection Jobs (or Administration > Data Gateway Management > Collection Jobs, depending on the build).
  5. On Bulk jobs, confirm system jobs are READY or Successful, not Failed.
  6. On Parameterized jobs, confirm default reachability jobs exist. Policy-driven and service-based jobs appear later, after you use performance policies and Service Health.

Result: You can point at the collector that feeds inventory, alarms, and utilization. You will read collection jobs in more detail in chapter 9.

docs.title: 2.4 What you leave alone
docs.text:
Credential profiles, AAA, certificates, backup jobs, and licensing are visible from Administration and from Device Management > Credential Profiles. Open a profile only if a device is unreachable and you need to compare the profile name.

Backup, restore, and Add OS patch put the cluster into maintenance mode. Patching is a guided walk in chapter 9. Do not start it here.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Platform Infrastructure, Optimization Engine, Active Topology, and element management are Healthy or Running.
  • The SR-PCE provider is reachable.
  • The NSO provider is reachable.
  • A Data Gateway (or embedded collector) is Up and the XR devices are attached.
  • Collection jobs are not in a Failed state.

docs.title: 3. Active Topology
docs.text:
Time: 45 minutes.

Objective: Use Crosswork Active Topology to answer where a device sits and how it is connected, then prove the same facts from IOS-XR CLI.

Active Topology is the map. Optimization Engine draws traffic-engineering objects on top of the same topology. You will use both views, then open a PE console from CML.

This lab is IPv6. IS-IS, BGP-LS, SRv6 locators, and PCEP should match what the map shows.

docs.title: 3.1 Open the map
docs.text:
1. From the main menu, open Topology.
  2. Wait for the devices from 5-nodes_L3VPN 8201-32FH 25.3.1-ipv6 to appear. An empty map usually means the SR-PCE provider is up and BGP-LS is still down, or the CML nodes are still booting. Recheck chapter 2.
  3. Use the logical map, not the geographical map.
  4. Identify two provider-edge routers. Those become the headend and the endpoint for chapters 5 through 8. Write the hostnames on your lab-values sheet.

Result: You can find both PEs and at least one IGP path between them.

docs.title: 3.2 Read a device and a link in CNC
docs.text:
1. Select the headend. Open the details panel.
  2. Record hostname, management IPv6 address, reachability, and IGP router id if it is shown.
  3. Select a core link on a path between the two PEs.
  4. In the link details, record:
    • Interface names on each side
    • IGP metric
    • TE metric, if one is shown
    • Utilization, if a value is shown
    • SRv6 adjacency or locator information, if the link shows it
  5. Open the layer or protocol selector. Turn on the IGP layer, then the SRv6 layer. Flex-Algo, if present, is a map fact in this lab, not a configuration task.

Utilization on a CML link is often 0%. Write down the number you actually see.

Result: One device record and one link record in your notes.

docs.title: 3.3 Confirm the same topology from XR CLI
docs.text: From CML, open a console on the headend PE. Stay in EXEC. Do not enter configuration mode.

docs.title: Neighbors and IGP
docs.text:
show isis neighbors
show isis topology

If the lab uses a named IS-IS instance, the instructor will give you the instance name and you will use:

show isis instance <name> neighbors
show isis instance <name> topology

Match each IS-IS neighbor to a node on the CNC map. The neighbor count and the path you traced in section 3.2 should agree.

docs.title: Addressing
docs.text:
show ipv6 interface brief
show interface <core-interface> brief

Confirm the core interface you clicked on the map is up/up and that the IPv6 address matches the link panel in CNC.

docs.title: SRv6
docs.text:
show segment-routing srv6 locator
show segment-routing srv6 sid

The locator prefix on the PE should match the SRv6 layer on the map. If the map shows a locator and the CLI does not, the topology feed is stale. Wait and refresh; do not configure a locator.

docs.title: How CNC learned this topology
docs.text:
On the PE:

show bgp link-state
show bgp link-state summary

On the SR-PCE (the second CML lab), if the instructor opens that console:

show pce ipv6 peer
show pce ipv6 topology summary

PCE should list the PEs as BGP-LS and PCEP peers. That is the feed behind the CNC map.

Result: Hostname, neighbor, core interface, and SRv6 locator agree between CNC and CLI.

docs.title: 3.4 Dashboard baseline
docs.text:
1. Return to the home page or the topology dashboard.
  2. Record the reachable-device count and the SR policy count.
  3. Zero SR policies is acceptable before chapter 5. You will compare the policy count after you create a PCE-initiated policy.

Result: You have a baseline count of devices and policies.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Both lab PEs are on the map and reachable.
  • show isis neighbors (or the named-instance form) matches the map.
  • The core interface and SRv6 locator you recorded in CNC appear in XR CLI.
  • You know the baseline SR policy count.

docs.title: 4. Element management
docs.text:
Time: 50 minutes.

Objective: Use CNC Element Management Functions the way an operations team already uses SolarWinds: node status, hardware inventory, configuration archive, alarms, and interface performance. Deploy nothing from this chapter.

Element Management Functions in CNC 7.2 cover device onboarding, inventory, faults, metrics, software images, configuration backup, and configuration templates. You will map each SolarWinds-style view to a CNC page, then open that page.

docs.title: 4.1 SolarWinds to CNC
docs.text:
PTA operations already watches the network in SolarWinds (NPM for status, inventory, and performance; NCM for configuration). CNC is not a replacement of every SolarWinds poller. It is the controller view of the same devices, with IGP and SR context that SolarWinds does not have.

What you do in SolarWinds Where you do it in CNC What is different Node list, ICMP/SNMP reachability Device Management > Network Devices CNC also shows the credential profile and the Data Gateway mapping that collection uses Hardware inventory (chassis, modules, serials) Device Management > Network Inventory Same idea: serial, product id, alarm badge on the part Network map Topology (chapter 3) CNC map is IGP/SRv6 from SR-PCE, not only Layer-3 discovery Alert console / trap viewer Alerts > Alarms and Events CNC splits system, network, and device alarms. An alarm stays until it clears; an event is a point in time Interface utilization and thresholds Device Management > Performance Policies, plus link utilization on the topology map CNC Optimization Engine colors links from collected counters. Performance Policies raise threshold-crossing alarms NCM config archive, compare, restore Device Management > Configuration Backup and Restore CNC can also backup on configuration change. Restore is out of scope for this lab NCM config change jobs / scripts Device Management > Configuration Templates Parameterized CLI (Apache Velocity). Different from NSO L2/L3VPN templates in chapters 6 and 7

Use the table as a translation layer. The rest of this chapter is the CNC side.

docs.title: 4.2 Network devices and inventory
docs.text:
1. Go to Device Management > Network Devices.
  2. Find the headend from chapter 3. Record operational state, reachability, and the credential profile name.
  3. Confirm a Data Gateway (or embedded collector) is associated with the device. A missing mapping is why inventory and counters stay empty.
  4. Go to Device Management > Network Inventory.
  5. Filter to the headend hostname or product family (NCS 8200 / 8201).
  6. Open the chassis, one route processor or line card, and one pluggable if the inventory has them.
  7. Read the alarm summary on that inventory row.

Result: You can walk from a hostname to a chassis and a module, the same way you would drill into a SolarWinds node.

A device that stays unreachable needs credentials, IPv6 reachability to the management address, and a booted CML node. Give a freshly started lab several minutes before you call it failed.

docs.title: 4.3 Configuration backup
docs.text:
CNC archives device configuration, compares two archives, and can restore. This lab uses the archive as a reader, like NCM config view.

  1. Go to Device Management > Configuration Backup and Restore.
  2. Find the headend.
  3. Open the latest archived configuration. Identify hostname and the segment-routing or IS-IS section.
  4. If two archives exist, open compare and name one difference, or state that they match.
  5. Leave Schedule backup and Restore unused.

Result: You have seen a real archived configuration for the headend.

Automatic backup on configuration change, when it is enabled under Device Management > Configuration Preferences, is what makes this archive useful after chapters 6 and 7. Read the preference. Leave the values as you found them.

docs.title: 4.4 Configuration templates (read only)
docs.text:
Device templates under Device Management are parameterized CLI. They are for repeating underlay or day-1 configuration. They are not the NSO L2VPN/L3VPN function-pack templates, and they are not the custom template you may attach to a VPWS in chapter 7.

  1. Go to Device Management > Configuration Templates.
  2. Open one existing template, if any exist. Read the device types it targets and one variable it expects.
  3. Close it. Leave Create Template and every deploy action unused.

Result: You can explain this store versus the NSO service template.

docs.title: 4.5 Alarms and events
docs.text:
1. Go to Alerts > Alarms and Events.
  2. Stay on Alarms. Use the category list to see system, network, and device alarms as separate sets.
  3. Filter to the headend if the filter allows it.
  4. If an alarm is present, record severity, source, and whether it is acknowledged. Leave acknowledge, clear, and annotate unused unless the instructor gives you a lab alarm of your own.
  5. Switch Show from Alarms to Events.
  6. Read the newest event. An event is a moment in time. An alarm remains until it clears.

Result: You can open both views. An empty alarm list is valid on a healthy CML lab. Write "no active device alarms" and move on.

You will use this page again in chapter 9.

docs.title: 4.6 Performance
docs.text:
Link colors on the topology map come from interface utilization collected for Optimization Engine. Element management adds polling policies, which is the CNC equivalent of a SolarWinds threshold on an interface.

  1. Go to Device Management > Performance Policies.
  2. Open one existing policy, if any exist. Read which devices it covers, how often it polls, and which threshold raises an alarm.
  3. Return to the headend in Network Devices or Network Inventory and open the metrics or interface view. Compare one interface counter with the utilization you wrote down in chapter 3.
  4. Leave the policy switch as you found it.

Result: You can say where a threshold is defined, and you can point at one live counter.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You can map node list, inventory, alerts, config archive, and utilization from SolarWinds to a CNC page.
  • The headend is in Network Devices and in Network Inventory.
  • You opened an archived configuration and did not restore it.
  • You opened Alarms and Events.
  • You compared one interface counter with the topology utilization from chapter 3.

docs.title: 5. SR-TE and SRv6
docs.text:
Time: 60 minutes.

Objective: Explain a PCC-initiated SRv6 policy that the headend already owns, then create one PCE-initiated SRv6 policy from CNC.

This CML topology is IPv6. Stay on the SRv6 tab in Traffic Engineering. Use SR-MPLS only if the instructor tells you the lab is not SRv6.

docs.title: 5.1 Words you need
docs.text: Term Meaning in this lab PCC The headend router. It can own a locally configured policy, and it has a PCEP session to SR-PCE. PCE SR-PCE in the second CML lab. It computes paths and can instantiate a policy on a headend through PCEP. PCC-initiated The policy configuration lives on the headend. CNC learns it from SR-PCE and draws it. PCE-initiated You create the policy in CNC. SR-PCE pushes it to the headend. The headend shows it as delegated to the PCE. Color A number that identifies the intent. Chapter 6 binds an L3VPN to this color. Candidate path One way to reach the endpoint. Preference chooses among candidate paths.

docs.title: 5.2 Find the PCC-initiated policy
docs.text:
The instructor may prepare one PCC-initiated policy on the headend before class. You do not type that router configuration.

  1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Traffic Engineering.
  2. Open the SRv6 tab.
  3. Find a policy whose initiation column says PCC. If none exists, record that and continue. The live create in this chapter is the PCE-initiated policy.
  4. Record headend, endpoint, color, preference, and the active candidate path.
  5. Select the policy and show it on the map. Name two hops on the drawn path.

Result: You can point at a policy the router owns, or you have recorded that none was prepared.

On the headend console:

show segment-routing traffic-eng policy
show segment-routing traffic-eng pcc ipv6 peer

Find the PCC policy color and the PCEP peer address. That peer should be the SR-PCE you checked in chapter 2.

On the SR-PCE, if the instructor opens it:

show pce ipv6 peer
show pce ipv6 lsp

The PCC session should be up. The LSP list should include the PCC-initiated policy when one exists.

docs.title: 5.3 Create a PCE-initiated policy
docs.text:
Use name pta-pce-01 and the color the instructor assigns. Do not reuse a color that already belongs to the PCC-initiated policy.

  1. Stay on Services & Traffic Engineering > Traffic Engineering, SRv6 tab.
  2. Start the create action and choose PCE-initiated.
  3. Set:
    • Name: pta-pce-01
    • Headend: the headend from chapter 3
    • Endpoint: the endpoint from chapter 3
    • Color: the instructor's value
    • Optimization objective: IGP metric, unless the instructor writes a different objective
  4. Leave bandwidth, affinity, and disjoint constraints empty unless the instructor adds one constraint.
  5. Preview the path. You want a path through the five-node core, from headend to endpoint.
  6. If the preview is empty, stop. An empty preview means SR-PCE has no SRv6 topology or no SID reachability. Recheck chapter 2 and the CLI in section 5.2. Do not commit an empty path.
  7. When the preview shows a path, provision the policy.
  8. Return to the policy table. Your row shows initiation PCE, your color, and an operational state that is up.
  9. Select the row and display the path on the map.

Result: A PCE-initiated SRv6 policy exists and the map draws it.

docs.title: 5.4 Confirm on the headend
docs.text:
show segment-routing traffic-eng policy
show segment-routing traffic-eng policy name pta-pce-01

Find pta-pce-01. If a PCC-initiated policy was prepared, it is still present. The difference is ownership: one policy is configured on the router, the other was instantiated by the PCE.

If your policy is missing on the router and present in CNC as down, check:

show segment-routing traffic-eng pcc ipv6 peer

A down PCEP session, a color conflict, or a headend that cannot place the SRv6 SIDs are the usual causes. Delete only pta-pce-01, and only if it is down and the instructor agrees.

docs.title: 5.5 Clean-up rule
docs.text: Keep this policy until chapter 6 has steered an L3VPN onto its color. At the end of the day, delete the VPNs first, then delete pta-pce-01. Leave any PCC-initiated policy in place.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You can say who owns the PCC-initiated policy (if one exists) and who owns pta-pce-01.
  • pta-pce-01 is up, with the assigned color, and it is drawn on the map.
  • show segment-routing traffic-eng policy on the headend lists your policy, and show segment-routing traffic-eng pcc ipv6 peer shows the PCE up.

docs.title: 6. L3VPN provisioning
docs.text:
Time: 60 minutes.

Objective: Create one L3VPN from CNC. NSO renders the device configuration from the IETF L3VPN network model. Steer the VPN onto the PCE-initiated SRv6 policy from chapter 5.

The UI path is Services & Traffic Engineering > Provisioning (NSO). You fill in the service intent. You do not paste CLI, and you do not edit the XML template on the NSO server.

docs.title: 6.1 What you are about to commit
docs.text:
Field Value Service name pta-l3vpn-01 Endpoints the two PEs from chapter 3, using the attachment points the instructor assigns Route distinguisher and route targets assigned by the instructor Steering preferred path, bound to the color of pta-pce-01 Transport SRv6

Preferred path is the steering method for this lab because the map can show the VPN sitting on the policy you created. On-demand next hop (ODN) is the other method: the headend builds a path when it receives a route with that color. Read the ODN choice in the form so you recognize it, then select preferred path unless the instructor names a different knob.

docs.title: 6.2 Create the service
docs.text:
1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Provisioning (NSO).
  2. Open the L3VPN service type.
  3. Create a service named pta-l3vpn-01.
  4. Select the instance profile or VPN profile the instructor named. That profile points at the NSO L3VPN template. You are choosing it, not editing it.
  5. Enter the route distinguisher and route targets for this lab.
  6. Add the two endpoints. For each endpoint set the device, the attachment circuit or interface, and the PE-CE routing the instructor specified. A lab that uses a static route on one side and BGP on the other is still one L3VPN.
  7. Set the underlay transport to SRv6.
  8. Set steering to preferred path and select the color of pta-pce-01, or select the policy name if the form asks for a policy.
  9. Run Dry run before Commit. Read the preview far enough to see your service name, your two endpoints, and the color.
  10. Commit.
  11. Open the service and read the sync state. In sync means NSO and the devices agree. Out of sync: use Check sync before you debug the VRF. Sync from is an optional exercise in chapter 7, not the first response here.

Result: pta-l3vpn-01 is committed and in sync.

docs.title: 6.3 See it on the map
docs.text:
1. Open Services & Traffic Engineering > VPN Services.
  2. Select pta-l3vpn-01.
  3. Show the service path and the underlay policy together.
  4. Confirm the underlay is pta-pce-01, or a path whose color matches that policy.

Result: You can show the L3VPN and the SRv6 policy it rides.

docs.title: 6.4 Read the effect on the PE
docs.text:
On the headend:

show vrf all
show bgp vpnv6 unicast summary
show bgp vpnv4 unicast summary

This core is IPv6. The VPN address family may still be VPNv4, VPNv6, or both. Use the family the instructor named. Then:

show segment-routing traffic-eng policy

You want a VRF for pta-l3vpn-01 (or the VRF name NSO assigned) and the same PCE-initiated policy as chapter 5. Leave configuration mode.

docs.title: 6.5 Templates, stated once
docs.text: The XML templates in the NSO L3VPN function pack turned your form into CLI. Device Management templates from chapter 4 did not. If a dry run fails with a template or profile error, the profile name is the thing to check.

docs.title: 6.6 Clean-up rule
docs.text: Keep this VPN until you have shown it on the map. Delete order at the end of the day is L2VPN, then L3VPN, then pta-pce-01. Deleting the policy first, while a VPN still prefers it, leaves the service with nowhere to steer.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Dry run showed your service name, your endpoints, and your color.
  • The service is in sync.
  • The VPN overlay draws pta-l3vpn-01 on pta-pce-01.
  • show vrf all on the PE lists the VRF NSO created.

docs.title: 7. L2VPN provisioning
docs.text:
Time: 60 minutes for VPWS. Optional sections add about 30 minutes.

Objective: Provision a point-to-point L2VPN (VPWS) from CNC. Optionally inspect VPLS, attach an NSO custom template, and run sync-from.

CNC 7.2 provisions IETF L2VPN network models through NSO. VPWS is a wire between two attachment circuits. VPLS is a multipoint LAN. This lab's required service is VPWS. Chapter 8 monitors that VPWS only.

docs.title: 7.1 VPWS (required)
docs.text:
Field Value Service name pta-vpws-01 vpn-type point-to-point / VPWS (use the value the form offers for two endpoints) Endpoints the two PEs from chapter 3, on the L2 attachment interfaces the instructor assigns Transport SRv6, preferably the same color or policy as pta-pce-01 if the form allows it

Do not reuse the L3VPN attachment interfaces from chapter 6. VPWS needs its own attachment circuits.

  1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > Provisioning (NSO).
  2. Open the L2VPN service type.
  3. Create a service named pta-vpws-01.
  4. Set vpn-id to a unique value the instructor assigns.
  5. Set vpn-type to the point-to-point / VPWS choice. Do not choose a multipoint or VPLS type here. If the form only lists mpls-evpn when you add more than two vpn-nodes, you have the wrong number of endpoints. VPWS uses two.
  6. Add two vpn-nodes. For each node set the device and the attachment circuit (interface, VLAN if the instructor specified one).
  7. Set underlay transport to SRv6. If preferred-path or ODN is offered, bind it the way the instructor specified. Preferred path onto pta-pce-01 is the consistent choice with chapter 6.
  8. Leave Custom-template empty for the required service. Optional section 7.3 uses that field on a copy, not on this one.
  9. Run Dry run. Confirm the service name, two endpoints, and vpn-type. Confirm it is not a VPLS.
  10. Commit.
  11. Open the service. Confirm it is in sync.

Result: pta-vpws-01 is committed and in sync.

docs.title: 7.2 Visualize and confirm from CLI
docs.text:
1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > VPN Services.
  2. Select pta-vpws-01. Show it on the map. You should see a point-to-point overlay between the two PEs, not a multipoint LAN.
  3. On the headend:
show l2vpn xconnect
show l2vpn xconnect detail

Find the xconnect NSO created. Attachment circuit and pseudowire (or SRv6 EVPN VPWS equivalent) should be up. If the lab uses EVPN VPWS, the instructor may also ask for:

show l2vpn evpn xconnect
show bgp l2vpn evpn summary

Use the form that actually prints your service. Leave configuration mode.

Result: The map is point-to-point, and XR shows the xconnect up.

docs.title: 7.3 Optional: VPLS
docs.text:
Do this section only if the instructor asks for it. Chapter 8 does not enable Service Health on a VPLS.

  1. In Provisioning (NSO), create a second L2VPN named pta-vpls-01.
  2. Choose the VPLS or multipoint vpn-type the form offers. Add at least two vpn-nodes (three if the instructor wants a true multipoint picture).
  3. Dry run, then commit.
  4. In VPN Services, select pta-vpls-01 and confirm the overlay is multipoint.
  5. On a PE:
show l2vpn bridge-domain

Use this only to contrast with show l2vpn xconnect from the VPWS. Delete pta-vpls-01 before the end of the day if you created it. Do not start Service Health on it.

Result: You can tell VPWS (xconnect) from VPLS (bridge-domain) in both CNC and CLI.

docs.title: 7.4 Optional: NSO custom template
docs.text:
An NSO custom template adds CLI that the L2VPN function pack does not model (for example an extra QoS or interface command). Templates must already exist in NSO. CNC only displays parameterizable fields.

  1. Ask the instructor for the template name, if one is loaded.
  2. Open pta-vpws-01 in edit, or clone it to pta-vpws-template-01 if you should not change the monitored service.
  3. In Custom-template, select the template. Fill the variables CNC shows.
  4. Dry run. Read the extra CLI the template adds.
  5. Commit only if the instructor wants the extra CLI on the device.
  6. If you only needed to see the fields, cancel without commit.

This is not a Device Management configuration template from chapter 4.

Result: You saw how a custom template attaches to a VPWS, and you know which store it lives in.

docs.title: 7.5 Optional: sync-from
docs.text:
NSO keeps a copy of device configuration. Check sync compares that copy with the device. Sync from pulls the device configuration into NSO. Sync to pushes NSO to the device. Redeploy reconcile rebuilds the service while keeping non-service configuration.

Use this on the VPWS only when the instructor wants the room to see out-of-sync handling. sync-from after a service commit can make the service look out of sync until you redeploy. That is the lesson, and it is easy to leave messy.

  1. On pta-vpws-01, open Actions.
  2. Run Check sync. Record in-sync or out-of-sync.
  3. Open Config view or View in NSO and read the service data.
  4. If the instructor has made a small out-of-band change on one PE, run Sync from.
  5. Run Check sync again. Expect out-of-sync if the device now differs from the service model.
  6. Run Redeploy dry run, then Redeploy reconcile only if the instructor wants the service model to win.

Do not run Sync to unless the instructor says so. Sync to overwrites the device with NSO's copy.

Result: You can say what Check sync, Sync from, Sync to, and Redeploy reconcile each do, and you used only the actions the instructor approved.

docs.title: 7.6 Clean-up rule
docs.text: Keep pta-vpws-01 through chapter 8. Delete optional VPLS and template clones first at the end of the day, then the VPWS, then the L3VPN, then the PCE-initiated policy.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• pta-vpws-01 is in sync and shown as point-to-point in VPN Services.
  • show l2vpn xconnect (or the EVPN form) lists the service.
  • Optional sections are either completed or marked skipped.

docs.title: 8. Assurance
docs.text:
Time: 40 minutes.

Objective: Enable CNC Service Health on the VPWS from chapter 7 and read Basic monitoring until the health column has a real state. Do not monitor VPLS.

Service Health scores a provisioned VPN against heuristic rules. For L2VPN it looks at VPWS xconnect state, device CPU and memory, and, in Advanced mode, interfaces, PCEP, SR policy, and path reachability. This lab uses Basic Monitoring on pta-vpws-01 only.

docs.title: 8.1 Find the VPWS
docs.text:
1. Go to Services & Traffic Engineering > VPN Services.
  2. Select pta-vpws-01.
  3. Confirm vpn-type is point-to-point / VPWS. If you also created pta-vpls-01 in chapter 7, leave it unmonitored.
  4. Confirm the service is in sync. Service Health on an out-of-sync service is not a useful baseline. Fix sync in chapter 7 before you start monitoring.

Result: You are looking at the VPWS, not the L3VPN and not a VPLS.

docs.title: 8.2 Start Basic monitoring
docs.text:
1. In the Actions menu for pta-vpws-01, choose Start monitoring.
  2. Set monitoring level to Basic Monitoring. Do not choose Advanced unless the instructor wants the extra subservices and you have time to wait. Switching levels can take more than 15 minutes before symptoms appear.
  3. Select the configuration profile the instructor names (often a Gold or Silver heuristic profile that is already loaded).
  4. Start monitoring.
  5. Wait. The Health column moves from Initiated to Good, Degraded, Down, or Not Monitoring.

Result: Health is no longer empty.

If Health stays on Initiated, collection for Service Health is still starting. Parameterized collection jobs of type service-based appear under Administration > Collection Jobs. You will read those jobs in chapter 9. Give Basic monitoring several minutes on this lab.

docs.title: 8.3 Read the health of the VPWS
docs.text:
1. Open pta-vpws-01.
  2. Read the Health state and the list of subservices. For Basic L2VPN / VPWS, expect rules that cover:
    • VPWS xconnect / control-plane health
    • Device health (CPU, memory)
    • ODN or SR policy health, if the service is bound to a policy
  3. Open one subservice. Read the metric that is Good or Degraded. Typical metrics are xconnect.state, attachment-circuit state, and pseudowire state.
  4. If Health is Degraded or Down, do not clear anything yet. Note the symptom, then confirm it on the PE:
show l2vpn xconnect
show l2vpn xconnect detail

A down attachment circuit on the router should match a down AC metric in Service Health. If CNC says Down and XR says Up, wait for the next collection cycle, then look at collection jobs in chapter 9.

  1. On the map, with the VPWS selected, confirm the overlay still terminates on the two PEs you provisioned.

Result: You can point at the heuristic result and at the matching XR xconnect state.

docs.title: 8.4 What you do not do in this chapter
docs.text:
• Do not start monitoring on pta-vpls-01 or on any multipoint L2VPN.
  • Do not start monitoring on pta-l3vpn-01 unless the instructor adds it as extra credit. The required assurance object is the VPWS.
  • Do not switch this VPWS to Advanced Monitoring after Basic has already started, unless the instructor wants to show the delay.
  • Do not stop monitoring until the instructor says the chapter is done. Stopping with "retain historical data" is available; use it only if you need to restart.

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• Service Health is running on pta-vpws-01 at Basic Monitoring.
  • You can name the Health state and one subservice or metric.
  • That metric agrees with show l2vpn xconnect (or you have recorded a collection lag).
  • No VPLS is being monitored.

docs.title: 9. Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Time: 45 minutes.

Objective: Collect CNC showtech, read collection jobs, read alarms, and walk the add-patch workflow. Applying a patch is an instructor decision because CNC puts itself into maintenance mode to install it.

This chapter is about the controller, not about rewriting router configuration.

docs.title: 9.1 Alarms
docs.text:
1. Go to Alerts > Alarms and Events.
  2. Filter Alarms by category: system, network, and device.
  3. For each category, record whether anything is raised. System alarms belong to CNC itself (disk, application, collector). Device alarms belong to the XR nodes.
  4. Open one alarm if any exist. Record severity, source, time, and description. Leave acknowledge and clear unused unless the instructor assigns that alarm to you.
  5. Switch to Events and find the event that created the alarm, if one exists.

Result: You know whether the platform, the network, or a device is currently unhappy.

Use alarms together with chapter 2 health tiles. A Healthy application tile and a system alarm can both be true; the alarm is the detail.

docs.title: 9.2 Collection jobs
docs.text:
Empty inventory, blank utilization, and Service Health stuck on Initiated are usually collection problems, not VPN problems.

  1. Go to Administration > Collection Jobs, or Administration > Data Gateway Management > Collection Jobs.
  2. Open Bulk jobs. These are created by the system, the UI, or the API. Record Status (READY, NOTREADY, FAILED) and collector type (SNMP, CLI, gNMI, syslog, trap).
  3. Open a Successful or READY job. Read the device list and the sensor path or CLI command.
  4. Open Parameterized jobs:
    • Default jobs — reachability
    • Policy-driven jobs — Performance Policies from chapter 4
    • Service-based jobs — created when you started Service Health on the VPWS
  5. Find a service-based job related to pta-vpws-01 or to L2VPN monitoring. Confirm it is not Failed.
  6. If a job is Failed or Degraded, open the job details and read the error. Common causes:
    • Device not attached to a Data Gateway
    • SNMP or CLI credentials wrong
    • Device unreachable (chapter 3 CLI will already have shown this)
    • Destination in Error, while collection still runs and increments an error count

Do not create a new bulk job in class. Do not delete a system job.

Result: You can point at the job that feeds Service Health, and you know whether it is READY.

docs.title: 9.3 Showtech
docs.text: Showtech is what you collect before you open a TAC case. CNC 7.2 collects cluster logs and metrics from Crosswork Manager. Application showtech is per application. Data Gateway showtech is a separate encrypted download.

docs.title: Cluster and application
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Crosswork Manager.
  2. Open Crosswork Summary > System summary.
  3. Click Actions and note the showtech options:
    • Request all — logs and metrics
    • Request metrics
    • Collect logs
  4. If the instructor wants a file from this VM, collect logs (not Request all) so the bundle stays smaller. Otherwise, only open Actions > View showtech jobs and read any previous job.
  5. To collect for one application, return to Crosswork Health, open the application tile (for example Service Health or Platform Infrastructure), and use that tile's showtech action. Application logs are collected separately from the cluster bundle.
  6. In View showtech jobs, read status. Publish or download only if the instructor will take the file. Delete nothing.

Result: You know where cluster showtech and application showtech are started, and you did not fill the disk unless the instructor asked for a collect.

docs.title: Data Gateway (read only unless asked)
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Data Gateway Management.
  2. Select the gateway.
  3. Open Actions and find Download Showtech.
  4. Do not download unless the instructor asks. The file is encrypted. The instructor keeps the passphrase and decrypts the file if TAC needs it. Do not put a passphrase in chat or in this guide.

Result: You can show where CDG showtech lives.

docs.title: 9.4 Add patch
docs.text:
CNC 7.2 installs OS security patches (SPACK) from System management. Application bundles are added from Application Management. Both are maintenance operations. Adding an OS patch automatically turns maintenance mode on, applies the bundle node by node, and turns maintenance mode off. Rollback is not supported. A small lab VM still takes a long time.

Instructor

Walk the screens with the room. Apply a patch only if a lab SPACK or application file is staged and you have time for maintenance to bounce. Students do not click Add unless you say so.

docs.title: OS patch screens
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Crosswork Manager.
  2. Open the System management tab.
  3. Find Add OS patch. Open the dialog far enough to see that the source is URL or SCP. Do not enter a server password into the guide or into a screenshot.
  4. Close the dialog unless the instructor is applying a staged patch.
  5. Open System updates (or the list of already installed patches). Record whether this dCloud image already shows 7.2.1-SP or another installed bundle.
  6. Open Job History on System management. This is where add-to-repository and per-VM apply jobs appear after someone adds a patch. Read any existing job. Do not retry a job unless the instructor is recovering a failed apply.
  7. After a successful apply (instructor only), verification is Administration > Crosswork Manager > System summary > View details > Package details.

If the instructor does apply a patch, wait. Do not log in while maintenance mode is on. When the UI returns, repeat the health checks from chapter 2.

docs.title: Application file
docs.text:
1. Go to Administration > Crosswork Manager > Application Management.
  2. Note Add new file. That is how an application CAPP or a patch bundle is uploaded.
  3. Do not upload a file unless the instructor provides one and asks you to.

Result: You can find Add OS patch, System updates, Job History, and Application Management. You did not start a patch on your own.

docs.title: 9.5 If something from an earlier chapter is still broken
docs.text: Symptom First check Empty topology SR-PCE provider, BGP-LS, show pce ipv6 topology summary Device unreachable in Network Devices CML node booted, management IPv6, credential profile Thin inventory / no utilization Data Gateway attachment, collection job status SR policy preview empty SRv6 tab, show segment-routing srv6 locator, PCEP peer VPN out of sync NSO provider, Check sync, then chapter 7 optional sync-from only if asked Service Health stuck on Initiated Parameterized service-based collection job

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You opened Alarms and Events and recorded what is (or is not) raised.
  • You found bulk and parameterized collection jobs, including a service-based job for the VPWS when monitoring is on.
  • You can start cluster showtech from System summary and you know that application and CDG showtech are separate.
  • You walked Add OS patch and Job History without starting an unplanned maintenance window.

docs.title: 10. Optional: CNC MCP server
docs.text:
Time: 20 minutes. Skip this chapter if the instructor does not start the assistant.

Objective: Ask the lab assistant one question that it can answer with a live Crosswork tool. Confirm the answer in the CNC UI. You decide what to do next.

The assistant is a chat page. When you ask a question, it may call tools on an MCP server. That server is what talks to CNC. The tools listed in the assistant sidebar are the only live data the assistant can fetch. Anything else in the reply is explanation until you confirm it in the UI.

docs.title: 10.1 Open the assistant
docs.text:
The instructor starts the assistant and the MCP server, then gives you the URL. You do not receive, and you do not type, the CNC password, an API token, or a client secret.

  1. Open the assistant URL.
  2. Read the backend status in the sidebar. Continue when it is online.
  3. Read the tool list. Find the tool whose description is the inventory node count. That is the live tool for this lab.
  4. If the sidebar also lists session or ticket tools, leave them unused. This chapter does not delete sessions and does not change the controller.

Result: The assistant is online and you can name the inventory tool.

docs.title: 10.2 One live question
docs.text:
In the chat, ask:

How many nodes are in the Crosswork inventory?

Wait for the reply. Open the tool-call detail for that turn.

Check all of the following:

  • The assistant called the inventory count tool.
  • The reply contains a number.
  • You can find a matching count under Device Management > Network Devices or Network Inventory. The two screens group equipment differently, so the numbers may differ by what each one counts. Write both numbers and one sentence on the difference. If they match, write that they match.

If the tool call fails, the useful symptom is the error text, not a second guess from the model. A failure here usually means the assistant cannot authenticate to CNC or cannot reach the UI address. That is an instructor fix. Chapters 2 and 4 already showed you the same inventory with your own login.

Result: A number from the tool, compared with Device Management.

docs.title: 10.3 Operator check, not a write
docs.text:
Ask a second question that does not require a write tool:

The inventory count is <the number you just verified>.
The CML lab should have the routers from 5-nodes_L3VPN 8201-32FH 25.3.1-ipv6.
What should an operator check first in Crosswork?

A useful answer names checks you already know how to open:

  • Reachability on Device Management > Network Devices
  • The credential profile on that device
  • Data Gateway mapping
  • Collection job status
  • SR-PCE and NSO provider status
  • Active alarms for that hostname

Take one check the assistant named, open that CNC page, and confirm or contradict the suggestion with the screen. The screen wins.

docs.title: 10.4 What you leave out of the chat
docs.text:
• Passwords, tokens, ticket ids, and certificate contents
  • A request to delete a session, a policy, a VPN, or a device
  • Configuration text from another service's dry run

docs.title: Done when
docs.text:
• You completed this chapter, or you skipped it because the assistant was not started.
  • If you used it: the assistant answered the inventory question with a tool call, and you compared that number with Device Management.
